g10-economics-ue8-t1.overview: Innovation is something new, improved or introduced that creates value, combining creativity with implementation. This lesson gives the Oslo Manual definition, presents the main types of innovation, and explains Schumpeter's idea of creative destruction.
objectives: Define innovation using the Oslo Manual definition
Identify the two key elements of innovation: creativity and implementation
Distinguish the main types of innovation and classify real examples
Explain eco-innovation and the two areas in which it creates value
Analyse creative destruction and its effects on firms and industries
g10-economics-ue8-t1.simple: Innovation is something new, improved or introduced that creates value. Its two key elements are creativity and implementation: you must think of a new idea and then put it into use. The Oslo Manual, the international reference guide of the OECD, defines innovation as a new or improved product or process that differs significantly from previous products or processes and is made available to potential users. The main types are organizational, process, product and marketing innovation, with eco-innovation linked to sustainable development goals. Innovation is also destructive: Schumpeter called this creative destruction, because new products and processes make old ones obsolete, close companies and create new industries. Only companies with a great strategic vision survive such episodes.
g10-economics-ue8-t1.detailed:
What innovation is. The Oslo Manual, an international reference guide from the OECD for collecting and using data on innovation, defines innovation as a new or improved product or process, or a combination of both, that differs significantly from the unit's previous products or processes and that has been made available to potential users (product) or brought into use by the unit (process). In simpler terms, innovation is something new, improved or introduced that creates value. Its two key elements are creativity, which produces the new idea, and implementation, which puts the idea to work.

What counts and what does not. A change must differ significantly from previous products or processes to be an innovation. A product innovation must be made available to potential users, but it does not need to generate sales; otherwise free digital products such as apps would be excluded. At the same time, routine changes or updates are not product innovations, because they only correct errors or make seasonal changes.

The main types of innovation. According to the 4th edition (2018) of the Oslo Manual, there are four main types. Organizational innovation is a new organizational strategy that changes business practices, workplace organization and relationships with external stakeholders, for example the first firms adopting a four-day working week or allowing employees to work from home. Process innovation implements a new or improved production or delivery approach, including changes in operational methods, techniques, equipment or software, such as the first firms betting on SaaS technology or the first hotels making decisions based on big data. Product innovation introduces a new or improved good or service, such as Lego changing its famous bricks to biodegradable oil-based plastics or the first electric vehicles and longer-range batteries in the car market. Marketing innovation develops a new marketing strategy producing changes in product design or packaging, or in decisions on price or promotion, such as Haagen Dazs' new waste-free container.

Eco-innovation. Eco-innovation is an innovation resulting in significant progress towards the 2030 sustainable development goals established by the UN. It reduces the impact of production modes on the environment, improves nature's resilience to environmental stresses, or achieves a more efficient and responsible use of natural resources. Eco-innovation creates value in two areas: it promotes sustainability throughout a product's life cycle, addressing climate change, resource scarcity and biodiversity, and it boosts a company's performance and competitiveness, helping it access new markets, increase productivity and profitability, strengthen its reputation and attract new investors. Examples include Procter and Gamble's cold-water detergents (product innovation), IKEA changing its fleet to electric vehicles (process innovation), and Nestle's paper-based straws replacing plastic ones (marketing innovation).

Creative destruction. Schumpeter (1934) argued that capitalism is a dynamic and innovative market system that is constantly changing. New ideas and processes take over the current paradigm and create new ways of producing goods and services or entirely new industries. He called this imbalance creative destruction, because innovation often leads to market chaos: products become obsolete, companies close and people become unemployed. He believed these are necessary consequences for new solutions that increase life quality to come to light. From the first industrial revolution to the petroleum boom and today's information society, periods of innovation make old models obsolete. Only companies with a great strategic vision survive an episode of creative destruction: Nokia and Kodak were once market leaders in their industries but failed to see how the cellphone and photography industries would change.

Famous innovators. The textbook lists Steve Jobs, who developed the smartphone world with the iPad; Marie Curie, who made great research on radioactivity; Elon Musk, who has made progress on luxurious electric cars; Nikola Tesla, who worked on the production, transmission and application of electric power; Thomas Edison, who invented the incandescent electric light bulb; Alexander Graham Bell, who invented the first telephone; Grace Hopper, who invented the first compiler for a computer programming language; and Leonardo DaVinci, who invented the parachute among many other things.

keyTerms.def: Something new, improved or introduced that creates value; summarized in two key elements: creativity and implementation.

Implementing a new or improved production or delivery approach, including changes in operational methods, techniques, equipment or software.

A new marketing strategy that changes product design, packaging, price or promotion.

Schumpeter's concept describing how new ideas and processes take over the existing status quo, making old products obsolete and creating new industries.

workedExamples.problem: A hotel group starts making its booking and pricing decisions using big data insights, while a rival hotel only repaints its rooms each season and fixes booking errors. Which hotel achieves process innovation?
workedExamples.given: Hotel A adopts big data for decision making; Hotel B repaints rooms seasonally and corrects errors.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: process innovation is a new or improved production or delivery approach; routine changes are not innovation.
workedExamples.substitution: Hotel A changed its decision-making approach using big data; Hotel B made only seasonal and corrective changes.
workedExamples.calculation: Hotel A's change is significant and affects how the service is delivered, so it is process innovation; Hotel B's changes are routine.
workedExamples.answer: Hotel A shows process innovation; Hotel B shows only routine changes.

workedExamples.problem: A coffee producer switches its export packaging to compostable paper and launches a promotion emphasizing the switch. Classify the innovations involved.
workedExamples.given: New packaging design plus a promotion built around it.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: marketing innovation changes product design, packaging, price or promotion.
workedExamples.substitution: The change affects packaging design and promotion rather than production methods.
workedExamples.calculation: Packaging and promotion changes fall under marketing innovation, and the compostable material also serves sustainability goals.
workedExamples.answer: Marketing innovation, with an eco-innovation dimension.

workedExamples.problem: A film company keeps producing only film cameras while digital photography spreads, and eventually loses all sales. Which concept explains this outcome?
workedExamples.given: An old product is overtaken by a new technology; a former market leader collapses.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: creative destruction makes old models obsolete while new solutions take over.
workedExamples.substitution: Digital photography is the new paradigm; the film camera becomes obsolete.
workedExamples.calculation: The company lacked the strategic vision to respond to disruption, like Kodak in photography and Nokia in cellphones.
workedExamples.answer: Creative destruction; firms that fail to innovate are displaced.

workedExamples.problem: An improvement to a free app adds a new function, but a paid app only receives a minor seasonal theme update. Which one is a product innovation?
workedExamples.given: App 1 gains a new function and is provided to users free; App 2 gets a seasonal update only.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a product innovation must add a new or improved function and be available to potential users; routine updates are excluded.
workedExamples.substitution: App 1 adds a function to a free product; App 2 makes only seasonal changes.
workedExamples.calculation: Sales are not required for product innovation, so the free app qualifies; the seasonal update does not differ significantly.
workedExamples.answer: App 1 is a product innovation; App 2 is only a routine update.

commonMistakes: Thinking innovation only means inventing completely new things; improved products and processes also count.
Confusing routine updates or error corrections with product innovation.
Believing a product must be sold, not just made available, to count as a product innovation.
Thinking creativity alone is innovation and forgetting the second element, implementation.
Believing creative destruction brings only harm; it is a necessary step for solutions that increase life quality.
Assuming big market leaders like Nokia and Kodak cannot fail when industries change.
applications: Classifying an Ethiopian bank's move to app-based services as process innovation.
Identifying product innovation when a local juice processor upgrades to biodegradable bottles.
Explaining how ride-hailing platforms disrupted traditional taxi services, an example of creative destruction.
Advising a shop to use marketing innovation by redesigning packaging for an export market rather than only advertising.
Discussing which Ethiopian industries could become obsolete if they ignore new technology.
Linking a firm's eco-innovation, such as renewable energy use, to lower costs and stronger reputation.
g10-economics-ue8-t1.summary: Innovation is something new, improved or introduced that creates value, restated by the Oslo Manual as a new or improved product or process made available to potential users. Its main types are organizational, process, product and marketing innovation, alongside eco-innovation tied to the 2030 sustainable development goals. Schumpeter's creative destruction shows that innovation both creates and destroys: old products become obsolete and firms like Nokia and Kodak that failed to adapt were lost.

g10-economics-ue8-t2.overview: A startup is a company in its initial stages of operations that expects significant growth in the near future, while a small business accepts a limited scale. This lesson distinguishes the two and explains how startups obtain seed funding from angel investors and venture capital.
objectives: Define a business startup and a small business
Differentiate startups from small businesses in growth and revenue goals
Explain why startups are usually not profitable in their initial stages
Describe seed funding and the role of angel investors and venture capital firms
Relate innovation and entrepreneurship to startup activity and market share
g10-economics-ue8-t2.simple: A startup is any company in the initial stages of operations that expects significant growth in the near future. A small business is any business with only a certain number of employees, a maximum that differs by industry. Startups focus on top-end revenue and growth potential and want to obtain as much market share as possible, while small businesses are content operating in a small portion of a large market. Startups are usually not profitable at first because they push rapid growth; it can take years to make the first dollar of profit. Because creating a viable product needs significant capital, startups raise seed funding: they approach angel investors who receive a share, usually 5-10 percent, of the business.
g10-economics-ue8-t2.detailed:
What a startup is. There are no strict guidelines that determine what a startup is, but the general definition is a company in the initial stages of operations that expects significant growth in the near future. The initial decisions made when forming a business will fuel early success or cause numerous hurdles at a time when the founder likely does not know how to navigate such problems. That is why understanding the difference between a startup and a small business matters before creating a company.

What a small business is. A small business is any kind of business that has only a certain number of employees, the maximum of which differs by industry. Such businesses may sound like startups, but they differ in one decisive way: small businesses are perfectly content operating in a small portion of a large market, while startups usually want to obtain as much market share as they can with the product or service they provide.

Growth and revenue. Startups are entirely different from small businesses when it comes to growth and revenue. A startup is considered a temporary business model focused on rapid growth. Unlike a small business, there are no restrictions or limitations placed on its growth; startups focus primarily on top-end revenue and growth potential. Their main goal is to create a product or service that can be successfully placed on the market, one that could bring in millions of dollars of profit in the long run. Among the most successful startups is Uber, which now has a market value of 50 billion dollars.

Profitability comes late. Startups will not be profitable in the initial stages of business development since they want to grow within the shortest time possible. It will sometimes take years for a startup to make its first dollar of profit. This is a deliberate trade-off: growth today is valued over profit today, in the expectation of much larger profits later.

How startups are funded. Because startups are attempting to create a product or service that is viable on the market, they need significant amounts of capital for product development, and this usually cannot be done without the right investments. In many cases startups obtain funding from angel investors or venture capital firms. Funding for most startups involves seed funding, which means the startup approaches potential angel investors for money. These investors are individuals who want to invest in a company they believe will eventually make it big, and in return they get a share of the business, usually equating to 5-10 percent.

Startups as sources of innovation. For many organizations, innovation is difficult to understand and execute, and there is a clear discrepancy between how big business and startups approach it. As a result, big business looks to startups and entrepreneurs to identify disruptive ideas and opportunities, and to unlock innovation through the spirit, blood, sweat and tears of entrepreneurship. This is why embracing the startup way of thinking matters for any economy that wants new products and services.

keyTerms.def: A company in the initial stages of operations that expects significant growth in the near future.
A business with only a certain number of employees, whose maximum differs by industry, content with a limited market portion.
The main focus of a startup, treated as a temporary business model aiming at the shortest possible time to scale.
The portion of total sales in a market captured by a firm's product or service.
The first money a startup raises by approaching potential angel investors to fund product development.
An individual who invests in a startup believed to eventually make it big, receiving a share, usually 5-10 percent.
A firm that invests money in startups needing significant capital for product development.
A person who starts and runs a business venture and bears its risks in pursuit of opportunity.

workedExamples.problem: Mekdes opens a neighbourhood shop serving her kebele, while Sara builds a delivery platform she plans to scale to every large city in the country. Which one is a startup?
workedExamples.given: Mekdes limits her goal to her neighbourhood; Sara expects significant growth and market capture.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a startup expects significant growth and maximal market share; a small business is content with a small portion of a market.
workedExamples.substitution: Sara's venture has a temporary business model focused on rapid growth; Mekdes' shop does not aim beyond its locality.
workedExamples.calculation: Only Sara's venture shows the growth expectation and market-share ambition that define a startup.
workedExamples.answer: Sara's delivery platform is a startup; Mekdes' shop is a small business.

workedExamples.problem: An angel investor gives a startup money in exchange for a 30 percent share. Is this within the typical range described in the lesson?
workedExamples.given: The investor receives 30 percent for seed funding.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: an angel investor's share for seed money usually equates to 5-10 percent.
workedExamples.substitution: 30 percent is three times the upper end of the typical 5-10 percent range.
workedExamples.calculation: The deal is far larger than the usual range, so the founder would surrender much more of the business than is typical.
workedExamples.answer: No. The usual angel share is 5-10 percent, so 30 percent is well above the standard.

workedExamples.problem: A founder promises investors quick profits in the first year from her new app startup. Evaluate this promise using the lesson.
workedExamples.given: The venture is a startup aiming at rapid growth of a new product.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: startups will not be profitable in the initial stages since they want to grow within the shortest time possible.
workedExamples.substitution: The goal is rapid growth and a viable product, not early profit.
workedExamples.calculation: It may take years for the first dollar of profit, so promising first-year profits contradicts how startups behave.
workedExamples.answer: The promise is unrealistic; startups usually sacrifice early profit for growth.

workedExamples.problem: A large company cannot find internally the disruptive ideas it needs. Where does the textbook say it should look, and why?
workedExamples.given: Big business struggles to execute innovation on its own.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: there is a clear discrepancy between how big business and startups approach innovation.
workedExamples.substitution: Startups and entrepreneurs identify disruptive ideas and opportunities.
workedExamples.calculation: By looking to startups, the big firm can unlock innovation through the spirit and risk-taking of entrepreneurship.
workedExamples.answer: It should look to startups and entrepreneurs, the natural source of disruptive ideas.

commonMistakes: Assuming every new business is a startup; small businesses have very different growth goals.
Expecting a startup to bring quick profits in the short run.
Believing small businesses want to grab as much market share as possible; that is the startup's aim.
Thinking a startup's growth is restricted like a small business; no restrictions are placed on startup growth.
Assuming seed funding is a grant; the angel investor receives a share of the business for the money.
Forgetting that small businesses have an employee maximum that differs by industry.
applications: Deciding whether a planned venture should be a small business serving one community or a startup aiming at national scale.
Preparing a pitch that explains the growth potential of the product to angel investors in Addis Ababa.
Explaining to family members why a new platform business may need years before its first profit.
Using the difference between startups and small businesses to avoid critical early mistakes in forming a company.
Noting how big firms in Ethiopia can source disruptive ideas from local startups and entrepreneurs.
g10-economics-ue8-t2.summary: A startup is a company in its initial stages that expects significant growth soon, while a small business accepts a limited scope and a defined employee maximum. Startups chase top-end revenue, market share and rapid growth, so they are rarely profitable in their first years, and Uber's 50 billion dollar value shows the possible payoff. To fund product development, startups raise seed money from angel investors and venture capital firms, giving investors typically a 5-10 percent share.

g10-economics-ue8-t3.overview: A form of business organization is the arrangement of ownership and management of a business, taking the forms of sole proprietorship, partnership and corporation. This lesson explains the features, advantages and disadvantages of each form.
objectives: Identify the three main forms of business organization
Explain the characteristics of a sole proprietorship, including unlimited liability
Describe the characteristics of a partnership, including limits on the number of partners
Explain why a corporation has a separate legal personality and limited liability for stockholders
Evaluate which form of business organization suits a given business scenario
g10-economics-ue8-t3.simple: Business organizations may be owned and managed by a single individual or by a group forming a partnership or a joint stock company; this arrangement of ownership and management is called a form of business organization. A sole proprietorship has one owner who provides the capital, bears the risk, takes all profits and losses, and has unlimited liability, so personal property can pay business debts. A partnership needs two or more persons, at most ten in banking and twenty in other businesses, who agree to share profits of a lawful business. A corporation has a separate legal personality from its owners; stockholders have limited liability but limited involvement, and a board of directors elected from the stockholders controls the activities of the corporation.
g10-economics-ue8-t3.detailed:
Forms of business organization. A business organization may be owned and managed by a single individual or by a group of individuals forming a partnership firm or a joint stock company. Such an arrangement of ownership and management is termed a form of business organization, and it usually takes three forms: sole ownership, partnership business and corporations.

Sole proprietorship. The term sole means single and proprietorship means ownership, so only one person owns the business. A sole proprietorship is a form of business organization in which a single individual owns and manages the business, takes the profits and bears the losses. This one person provides the capital, bears the risk and manages the business according to his or her own skill and intelligence. It is very simple to establish: any person willing to start a business with the necessary resources can set it up, and practically no legal formalities are required. In some cases, however, such as restaurants and chemist shops, permission from the competent authority must be obtained before starting. Its characteristics are: single ownership; no separation of ownership and management; few legal formalities; no separate entity, since the businessman and the business are one and the same; no sharing of profit and loss; unlimited liability, so if business assets are not enough to pay business liabilities, personal property can be used, and one-man control.

Sole proprietorship advantages and disadvantages. Advantages include being easiest to get started, greatest freedom of action and flexibility in operation, maximum authority, income tax advantages in very small firms, maintenance of business secrets, quick decision and prompt action, and a personal touch with customers. The disadvantages are limited resources, lack of continuity, unlimited liability, unsuitability for large scale operations, and limited managerial expertise.

Partnership. A partnership is a business owned by two or more persons who contribute resources into the entity and divide the profits among themselves. At least two persons are required; the maximum is ten for banking business and twenty for other businesses, and beyond these limits the partnership becomes illegal. Partnership is created by an agreement among persons competent to contract, so minors, lunatics and insolvent persons are not eligible to become partners, though a minor can be admitted to the benefits of the firm, sharing profits without any obligation for losses. The business must be lawful: an agreement to share profit from smuggling or black marketing is not a partnership in the eyes of law. Every partner is both principal and agent of the firm, and partners have unlimited liability, jointly and individually, so if the firm's assets are insufficient, the personal properties of the partners can be used. In general partnerships all partners have unlimited liability, while in limited partnerships creditors cannot go after the personal assets of the limited partners; the liability of a minor partner is limited to his share of the profits.

Registration, advantages and limits of partnership. Registration of a partnership firm is not compulsory, but an unregistered firm suffers limitations that make registration virtually compulsory: it cannot sue outsiders although outsiders can sue it; disputes among partners cannot be settled through a court of law; and the firm cannot claim adjustments for amounts payable to or receivable from other parties. Partnership advantages are easy formation, availability of larger resources, better decisions, flexibility, sharing of risks, benefits of specialization, protection of interest and secrecy. Its limitations are unlimited liability, instability, limited capital, non-transferability of shares and the possibility of conflicts.

Corporations. A corporation is a business organization that has a separate legal personality from its owners. Ownership in a stock corporation is represented by shares of stock. The owners, called stockholders, enjoy limited liability but have limited involvement in the company's operations; the board of directors, an elected group from the stockholders, controls the activities of the corporation. A corporation has all the legal rights of an individual, except the right to vote and certain other limitations, and the right to exist is given by the state that issues its charter. Among the basic forms of business ownership, these other types of organizations are also common today.

keyTerms.def: The arrangement of the ownership and management of a business, such as sole ownership, partnership or corporation.
A form of business organization in which a single individual owns and manages the business, takes the profits and bears the losses.
Personal responsibility of the owner or partners for business debts, so personal property can be used to pay business liabilities.
A business owned by two or more persons who contribute resources and divide the profits among themselves.
A partnership in which all partners have unlimited liability for the debts of the firm.
A partnership in which creditors cannot go after the personal assets of the limited partners.
A business organization with a separate legal personality from its owners, whose ownership is represented by shares of stock.
An elected group from the stockholders that controls the activities of the corporation.

workedExamples.problem: Ato Kebede wants to open a small restaurant in town with his own savings, managing it himself. Which form of business organization suits him, and what legal point must he remember?
workedExamples.given: One owner, own capital, personal management; the business is a restaurant.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a sole proprietorship is owned and managed by one person and needs almost no legal formalities.
workedExamples.substitution: Kebede is a single owner providing capital and bearing risk, exactly matching the sole proprietorship definition.
workedExamples.calculation: However, some businesses like restaurants and chemist shops require permission from the competent authority before starting.
workedExamples.answer: A sole proprietorship; he must obtain permission from the competent authority for the restaurant.

workedExamples.problem: Twenty-one traders want to form a partnership firm for a textile wholesale business. Can they legally do so?
workedExamples.given: The group has 21 persons; the business is not banking.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the maximum number of partners is ten for banking business and twenty for other businesses.
workedExamples.substitution: For a non-banking business the limit is 20, and the group has 21 members.
workedExamples.calculation: 21 exceeds the limit of 20, so the relationship among them cannot be called a legal partnership.
workedExamples.answer: No. A partnership of 21 persons in a non-banking business is illegal.

workedExamples.problem: A sole proprietor's business assets are worth 50,000 birr, but business debts are 120,000 birr. What happens to his debt burden?
workedExamples.formula: Principle: the liability of a sole proprietor is unlimited; personal property can pay business liabilities.
workedExamples.substitution: The business assets cover only 50,000 of the 120,000 birr owed, leaving 70,000 birr unpaid.
workedExamples.calculation: Because there is no separate entity, the owner's personal property can be used to pay the remaining 70,000 birr.
workedExamples.answer: His personal property can be used to pay the remaining 70,000 birr of business debt.

workedExamples.problem: Two friends want to start a firm with larger resources, shared risks and better decisions but without the complex charter of a big company. Which form should they choose and why?
workedExamples.given: Two owners; goals are larger resources, risk sharing and better decisions.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a partnership pools resources of two or more persons who share profits, losses and decisions.
workedExamples.substitution: A partnership offers larger resources, better decisions and shared risks, and is easy to form.
workedExamples.calculation: Compared to a sole proprietorship, which has limited resources and one view, the partnership matches all three goals; a corporation would involve shares of stock and a board of directors.
workedExamples.answer: A partnership, because it combines larger resources, better decisions and shared risks with easy formation.

commonMistakes: Thinking a sole proprietorship requires many legal formalities; practically none are required.
Believing the sole proprietor's personal property is safe from business debts; unlimited liability says otherwise.
Saying a partnership may have any number of partners; the limit is ten in banking and twenty in other businesses.
Assuming partnership registration is compulsory; it is voluntary, but an unregistered firm cannot sue outsiders.
Believing a corporation and its owners are the same legal person; the corporation has a separate legal personality.
Thinking stockholders run daily operations; the board of directors controls the corporation.
Forgetting that minors can be admitted to the benefits of a partnership even though they cannot be partners.
applications: A young person choosing a sole proprietorship for a corner juice stall because it is easiest to get started.
Relatives pooling money for a grain trade by forming a partnership with a written agreement.
A growing company needing large capital turning into a corporation that issues shares of stock.
Checking the legal maximum of partners before a group of farmers forms a poultry partnership.
Advising a friend to register the partnership so the firm can sue outsiders and settle disputes in court.
Weighing unlimited liability against quick decision making when selecting a form of organization.
g10-economics-ue8-t3.summary: The form of business organization is the arrangement of ownership and management, and it usually takes three forms. A sole proprietorship has one owner with quick decisions and all profits but limited resources and unlimited liability. A partnership of two or more, up to ten in banking and twenty otherwise, shares risks and resources but remains unstable with unlimited liability, while a corporation has a separate legal personality with stockholders enjoying limited liability and a board of directors in control.

right.name: Limited partnership
items: Creditors cannot take their personal assets
Still needs two or more partners

questions.q: What term describes the arrangement of ownership and management of a business?
questions.explanation: Such arrangement of ownership and management is termed a form of business organization.

questions.q: Sole ownership businesses are owned and managed by more than two individuals.
questions.explanation: Sole means single: only one person is the owner of the business organization.

questions.q: The maximum number of persons allowed in a banking partnership is:
questions.explanation: The maximum limit is ten for banking business and twenty for other businesses.

questions.q: In case of loss, if a sole proprietor's business assets are not enough to pay business liabilities:
options: Personal property can be used to pay them
questions.explanation: The liability of a sole proprietor is unlimited, so personal property can pay business liabilities.

questions.q: Why can a creditor claim a partner's personal property to settle firm debts?
questions.answer: partners have unlimited liability|jointly and individually liable
questions.explanation: Partners are jointly and individually liable, so personal properties can be used when firm assets are insufficient.

questions.q: Which of the following persons is NOT eligible to become a partner?
questions.explanation: Persons must be competent to contract, so minors are not eligible, though a minor may share in the profits.

questions.q: Which limitation applies to an unregistered partnership firm?
questions.explanation: An unregistered firm cannot sue outsiders, although outsiders can sue it.

questions.q: In a limited partnership, creditors cannot go after:
options: The personal assets of the limited partners
questions.explanation: In limited partnerships, creditors cannot go after the personal assets of the limited partners.

questions.q: A corporation has a separate legal personality from its owners.
questions.explanation: A corporation is a business organization that has a separate legal personality from its owners.

questions.q: Explain what limited liability means for stockholders of a corporation.
questions.answer: liability limited to their investment|personal property is protected|shares of stock limit loss
questions.explanation: Stockholders enjoy limited liability, meaning they cannot lose more than their investment in shares.

questions.q: Arrange the three forms of business organization from the fewest owners to the most.
questions.explanation: The order is: sole proprietorship (one), partnership (two or more), corporation (stockholders).

g10-economics-ue8-t4.overview: A proof of business concept, or feasibility study, tests whether a business idea warrants further investment before any business plan is written. This lesson distinguishes feasibility studies from business plans, lists the content of an SME feasibility study, and explains cost benefit analysis with the benefit/cost ratio.
objectives: Distinguish a feasibility study from a business plan in purpose and cost
State the five questions a feasibility study should answer
List the contents of an SME feasibility study, from business idea to market analysis
Explain cost benefit analysis and its three steps, including intangible costs and opportunity cost
Use the benefit/cost ratio to judge whether a business decision should proceed
g10-economics-ue8-t4.simple: Never commission a business plan until a feasibility study has been completed first. A feasibility study, also called a proof of business concept, normally costs less than 20 percent of a business plan and shows whether a project is feasible before major financial burden is incurred. It answers five questions: will it work, is it profitable, what will it basically cost, is it worth doing, and is it worth commissioning a business plan? An SME feasibility study covers the business idea, profiles of key people, personal objectives, the market and the business overview. When testing viability, entrepreneurs use cost benefit analysis, a process that weighs the sum of benefits of an action against its costs, including intangible items and opportunity cost, using the benefit/cost ratio.
g10-economics-ue8-t4.detailed:
Feasibility first. A lot of time, resources and money can be saved by knowing what to do and in what order. A good rule of thumb is to never commission a business plan until a feasibility study has been completed first. A proof of business concept, also known as a feasibility study, is normally less than 20 percent of the cost of a business plan. Although it is not the in-depth nuts and bolts view of a business plan, it does exactly what the name implies: it shows if a project is feasible before any other steps are taken or major financial burden is incurred.

What a feasibility study is. A feasibility study is designed to discover if a business or project is feasible: in short, does it warrant further investment of time, money and study, or is it a non-starter? It is a relatively inexpensive way to safeguard against wasting further investment. If the project is seen to be feasible, the next logical step is a full business plan, and the money spent on the study is not wasted because its research and information reduce the research time and therefore the cost of the business plan. The study is done quickly in general format and typically contains financial projections, a general description of the business, details of how the company will be formed, managed and marketed, statements about the competition, and a cash-flow projection based on averages. A feasibility study should answer five questions: 1. Will it work or not? 2. Is it profitable or not? 3. What will it basically cost to fund or start? 4. Is it worth doing? 5. Is it worth commissioning a business plan?

What a business plan is. A business plan is a detailed road map for building a given company. It contains all that the feasibility study has, plus specific timelines, detailed budgets with forecasts, letters of intent, resumes of staff, background, competition, strengths and weaknesses, work sheets with full supporting references, and appendices holding copies of key documentation. It shows exactly what revenues to expect and when, what overheads and expenses will be due, staffing levels and salaries, setup and building costs, and utility, legal, insurance and accounting costs. Business plans are commissioned for one of three reasons: re-organization, investment or funding, or a management blueprint for operation. People never plan to fail; people only fail to plan.

Developing an SME feasibility study. A formalized, written evaluation of the idea should show what facts and figures are needed for decision-making, whether the idea is viable, and alternative approaches to putting the idea into practice. It is written by you, for you, and should include: 1. The business idea: describe it so anyone knows exactly what it is, how it differs from existing businesses and who will buy; simply saying a coffee shop is not enough. 2. Profiles of key people: one-page resumes showing strengths, skills, experience and qualifications, revealing management strengths and missing skills. 3. Personal objectives: short term up to one year, medium term one to three years, long term greater than three years, since business is a means of achieving a home, cars, holidays and a good lifestyle. 4. The market: list potential customers and why they will buy, identify market segments and how often and how much they will buy, list products and services with costs and selling prices, identify preferred and alternative suppliers, and list competitors with two good points and two bad points each, remembering that price is not the only way to attract their customers. Obtain a map to define market boundaries, location and competitors. 5. Business overview: the site, whether rented, owned or at home, and the advantages and disadvantages of that location.

Function of a feasibility plan. Feasibility plans help entrepreneurs and their investors judge whether a business concept is credible. Preparing one is a testing and validation process to determine what could go wrong and what needs to go right for the enterprise to root and grow, and it often leads to significant changes in the original idea. The plan is not a formal document but a structured formal commercial report, your first reality check before the marketplace delivers the real check. In the feasibility plan the focus is on getting the design right and testing its coherence, not on convincing investors, so clarity and factual evidence matter more than a convincing business presentation.

Cost benefit analysis. A cost benefit analysis (CBA) is a process used primarily by businesses that weighs the sum of the benefits, such as financial gain, of an action against the negatives, or costs, of that action. It often incorporates monetary values for intangible benefits as well as opportunity cost into its calculations, and it is most often used for long-term decisions, although it also serves short-term ones. It takes indirect benefits and costs into consideration, like customer satisfaction and employee morale. CBA is similar to net present value (NPV), a method used to determine the benefits of an investment by calculating future benefits or costs in terms of their present value; given long-term views, the value of money changes with inflation, so NPV is used within CBA to calculate net present costs and benefits. If NPV is positive, the action is generally a good investment. For a standard CBA the formula, the benefit/cost ratio, is simply b/c, and the steps are: 1. Compile comprehensive lists of all costs and benefits, including intangible items and opportunity costs. 2. Give the costs and benefits a monetary value, even for indirect items such as lost working time during software installation. 3. Set up the equation and compare: if the sum of fiscal benefits outweighs the costs, proceed with the decision; otherwise re-examine and adjust. The equation can be set up for several options to compare them side by side.

keyTerms.def: A proof of business concept designed to discover whether a business or project is feasible before further investment.
A detailed road map for building a company, containing everything in the feasibility study plus timelines, detailed budgets, forecasts and appendices.
Another name for a feasibility study; it validates the idea and can become a supporting appendix of the business plan.
A process that weighs the sum of the benefits of an action against the costs of that action, including intangible items and opportunity cost.
The simple formula for standard CBA, written b/c, comparing total benefits with total costs.
A method that calculates future benefits and costs in terms of their present value; a positive NPV means the action is generally a good investment.
The value of the next best option given up when choosing a course of action, factored into a CBA.
A group of potential customers with similar buying patterns, identified when analysing the market in a feasibility study.

workedExamples.problem: An entrepreneur has a business budget for documents of 10,000 birr. Following the rule of thumb, roughly how much should she expect to spend on the feasibility study compared with the business plan?
workedExamples.given: Total document budget: 10,000 birr; a feasibility study is normally less than 20 percent of the cost of a business plan.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: feasibility study cost is less than 20 percent of business plan cost, and the two are separate documents.
workedExamples.substitution: If the plan costs about 8,400 birr, the study would be under 1,700 birr, for example about 1,600 birr.
workedExamples.calculation: About 1,600 birr for the study leaves about 8,400 birr for the plan, and 1,600 is less than 20 percent of 8,400.
workedExamples.answer: Roughly 8,400 for the plan and under 1,700 for the study; the study always comes first and is far cheaper.

workedExamples.problem: Selam proposes a milk delivery service in her town. Show how she would answer the five feasibility study questions.
workedExamples.given: Idea: delivering fresh milk to households; data on demand, costs and competition must be gathered.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: a feasibility study answers five questions: will it work, is it profitable, what will it cost to fund, is it worth doing, and is it worth commissioning a business plan?
workedExamples.substitution: Question 1: yes, households in the town buy milk daily. Question 2: projected revenue exceeds projected costs on average cash-flow figures. Question 3: about 60,000 birr for a fridge, containers and a supplier contract. Question 4: yes, it matches her personal objective of steady self-employment. Question 5: yes, the numbers justify a full business plan.
workedExamples.calculation: All five answers come out positive from the basic data, notes and meetings of the study.
workedExamples.answer: The concept proceeds to a full business plan because all five feasibility questions are answered favourably.

workedExamples.problem: A shop compares installing software worth 30,000 birr against renting a delivery motorbike worth 20,000 birr a year. Expected yearly gains are 50,000 birr from the software and 26,000 birr from the motorbike. Which option should the shop choose using cost benefit analysis?
workedExamples.given: Software: benefit 50,000, cost 30,000. Motorbike: benefit 26,000, cost 20,000.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: compare the benefit/cost, b/c, of each option and proceed only where benefits outweigh costs.
workedExamples.calculation: Both options are above 1, but 1.67 is greater than 1.3, so the software creates more benefit per birr of cost.
workedExamples.answer: Choose the software, since its b/c ratio of 1.67 beats the motorbike's 1.3.

workedExamples.problem: Marta wants a car within one year, a house in two to three years, and a farm business beyond three years. Classify her personal objectives in the feasibility study.
workedExamples.given: Car: within 1 year. House: 2-3 years. Farm business: beyond 3 years.
workedExamples.formula: Principle: personal objectives are short term up to one year, medium term one to three years, long term greater than three years.
workedExamples.substitution: The car falls in the short term, the house in the medium term and the farm business in the long term.
workedExamples.calculation: Each target is matched to the time band that the feasibility study requires.
workedExamples.answer: Short term: car. Medium term: house. Long term: farm business.

commonMistakes: Commissioning a business plan before completing a feasibility study, the opposite of the rule of thumb.
Treating the feasibility study and business plan as the same document; they are totally separate documents with different costs.
Thinking the money spent on a feasible study is wasted; the research reduces the time and cost of the business plan.
Ignoring intangible costs and benefits such as customer satisfaction, employee morale and opportunity cost.
Describing a business idea loosely as just a service business or a coffee shop instead of painting a clear picture.
Assuming price is the only way to attract customers away from competitors.
Believing the feasibility plan is mainly for impressing investors; its focus is getting the design right and testing coherence.
applications: Testing a student poultry or snack project with the five feasibility questions before borrowing money from a microfinance institution.
Using cost benefit analysis to compare buying a delivery motorbike against renting one for a small shop.
Drawing a map of market boundaries, competitors and suppliers before opening a snack shop in a new kebele.
Writing one-page profiles of each team member before approaching a lender or partner.
Setting short, medium and long term personal objectives before starting a family business.
Explaining why banks and investors require a business plan with timelines and detailed budgets, not just an idea.
g10-economics-ue8-t4.summary: A feasibility study is a cheap proof of business concept, usually less than 20 percent of a business plan's cost, and it must be completed before any business plan is commissioned. The business plan is a detailed road map containing timelines, detailed budgets and appendices, commissioned for re-organization, investment or funding, or operation. Finally, cost benefit analysis weighs total benefits against total costs, including intangible items and opportunity cost, using the benefit/cost ratio to decide whether to proceed.
